text: Τὰ μετάφρενα. Sunt quæ alii vocant μεταχένια. Suid. ὁ μεταξὺ τῶν ὤμων τόπος: Locus inter humeros: terga, dorsum. Suppletque Portus, quod a tergo præcordiis est objectum: sumpsitque ex Vaticano, cujus hæc sunt verba, Μετάφρενα. τὰ νῶτα, ὅτι ἐξόπισθεν τῶν φρενῶν κεῖται· φρένες δὲ, ὑμένες εἰσὶ μεταξὺ τῆς καρδίας καὶ τοῦ ἥπατος· Quod retro τῶν φρενῶν posita sunt: φρένες enim membranæ sunt inter cor. et jecur. Τὸ, ἐν χλωρότητι χρυσίου, quod Syxt. interpres reddere maluit, Hilarium secutus et August., in viriditate auri, quam quod Vulg. reddiderat, non probo. Liquet enim virorem et viriditatem non apte dici de auro (quidquid Hilarius, vigorem quemdam æternum putet ea voce significari), sed potius fulvorem et pallorem, qui auri color optimus est: auctor enim Galenus χλωρὸν ἀντὶ ὠχροῦ sumi; nec Hyppocrates aliter usurpat. Plinius quoque sic accepit apud Dioscorid. lib. iii, cap. 79, De Smyrnio, φλοιὸν ἔχουσα ἔξωθεν μὲν μέλανα, ἔνδοθεν δὲ χλωρὸν ἢ ὑπόλευκον· ipse sic vertit lib. xxvii, cap. 13: Cortex ejus foris niger, intus pallidus. Cum viride saturum significare volunt auctores, πρασοειδὲς vocare solent, et ὡσεὶ πράσον, quasi porro simile, convenitque quibusdam lapillis et herbis; auro, nunquam.
anchorLine: ρί· τὰ δὲ νοούμενα, φημὶ δὴ τὰ μετάφρενα (a),
en: Metaphrena: some call these metaxenia (sic). Suidas: the place between the shoulders, i.e. the region between the shoulders: the back, the dorsum. Portus adds: what lies behind the midriff; and he took it from the Vatican codex, whose words are: 'Metaphrena: the back, because it lies behind the phrenes; the phrenes are membranes between the heart and the liver.' That is, the parts situated behind the phrenes: for the phrenes are membranes between heart and liver. As for 'in the greenness (chlorotes) of gold,' which the Sixtine translator preferred to render, following Hilary and Augustine, 'in the viridity of gold,' rather than the Vulgate's rendering, the editor does not approve. For it is clear that verdure and greenness are not aptly said of gold (whatever Hilary may think, that some eternal vigor is signified by that word), but rather its yellow and pallor, which is the best colour of gold: for Galen is the authority that chloron is taken for ochron (pale); nor does Hippocrates use it otherwise. Pliny too understood it so in Dioscorides, book iii, ch. 79, on Smyrnium: 'having a bark black outside, chloron or whitish within'; he himself renders it, book xxvii, ch. 13: 'Its bark is black outside, pale inside.' When writers mean to signify a deep green they usually say leek-green (prasoeides), and 'as if leek-like'; it suits certain stones and herbs, never gold.

text: Καὶ ὡς ῥοθίζας κινήσεις. Quin sit mendum in illa voce, nullus dubito. Sit forte ῥοθίας, vel ῥοθιαζούσας, quod etiam verbum agnoscit Hesych. quasi tremente fluctus commotiones procellamque; ut alia aliam vocem Maximus explicet. Hoc enim præstant maris elationes, ut fluctus sic impetu assurgentibus, tumque eadem vi subsidentibus, aliisque alios intercipientibus ac se mutuo collidentibus, allisisque ad littora ipsasque rupes ac cautes, strepitus ejusmodi ac fragor procul reboet, qui terrorem ac stuporem injiciat: quæ omnia quasi alio in mari procul considerat, qui ipse in tranquillo contemplationis mari, velut ad clavum quiete sedens illique indormiens, vehitur.
anchorLine: πῶν μετεωρισμοὺς, καὶ ὡς ῥοθίζας κινήσεις (b), τὰ
en: 'And as [he considers] ῥοθίζας motions.' I have no doubt that there is an error in that word. Perhaps it should be ῥοθίας, or ῥοθιαζούσας, a verb Hesychius also recognizes: as if 'trembling commotions of the waves' and storm; so that Maximus would explain one word by another. For the swellings of the sea produce this: the waves rise with such force, then sink with the same force, others cutting off others and dashing against one another and thrown against the shores and the very rocks and reefs, so that such a noise and crash resounds from afar, which strikes terror and stupor. All this he observes as though in another sea, far off, he who himself is carried on the tranquil sea of contemplation, sitting quietly at the helm, as it were, and sleeping there.

text: Μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ἡγεμονικοῦ. Quem Maximus spiritum ἡγεμονικὸν hic vocat, ipse est quem Paulus Ephes. iv, 21, spiritum τοῦ νοὸς (mentis) vocat, et hortatur eo renovari; quod mens ipsa τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν in homine sit: quod scilicet in eo principale est ac imperio pollet: quæ, cum ipsa ex se fixa sit veri contemplatione, orationem ea fultam constantem, uniusque rationis (μονολόγιστον) reddat: τὸ προαιρετικὸν vero (velut dicas, arbitrarium) voluntatem, quæ pro hoc statu instabilis sit, exque alia in aliam mutatur pro rerum objectarum ac cogitationum varietate, inque eas affectione.
anchorLine: ματος ἡγεμονικοῦ (c) · ἄνευ δὲ θεωρίας, ὡς σάρξ
en: 'With the governing spirit.' The spirit that Maximus here calls 'hegemonic' is the very one Paul, in Ephesians iv, 21, calls the spirit of the mind, and he urges that we be renewed by it; for the mind itself is the hegemonic part in man, that is, it is the principal part in him and holds sway. When it is itself fixed on the contemplation of the truth, it makes prayer supported by it steady and of a single reasoning (monologiston). But the 'elective' faculty (as one might say, the arbitrary), that is the will, which in this state is unstable and shifts from one thing to another according to the variety of the objects and thoughts presented, and to the affection toward them.

text: Σαρκὶ παραμένειν. Græca vulgata, ἐπιμένειν ἐν τῇ σαρκί. Habent tamen codex Alexandrinus et Chrysost. in Expositione, ἐπιμένειν σαρκὶ, absque propositione, quæ nec admodum necessaria est, cum ejus vim habeat verbum compositum, sitque idem ἐπιμένειν atque ἐμμένειν· τὸ, παραμένειν Maximi magis respuit, habetque emphasin: permanere in carne, nec ab ea disjungi.
anchorLine: εὐδοκεῖ μᾶλλον σαρκὶ παραμένειν (d) · καὶ διὰ τὴν
en: 'To remain with the flesh.' The common Greek text reads 'to abide in the flesh.' Yet the Alexandrian codex and Chrysostom in his Exposition have 'to abide (with) the flesh' without the preposition, which is hardly necessary, since the compound verb carries its force, and 'epimenein' is the same as 'emmenein.' The 'paramenein' of Maximus rather rejects the preposition and has emphasis: to remain in the flesh and not be separated from it.

text: Νεοτελὴς νοῦς. Quasi recens ad perfectionem initiatus, eamque novum adeptus; etsi necdum in illa satis probatus. Suid. νεοτελής, νεωστὶ τετελειωμένος· quod Thesaurus Hesychio ascribit, cum sit solum Suidæ, redditque. Recens absolutus: non satis bene Portus, Recens confectus. Vox enim illa, qua una Suid. alteram explicavit, quamdam absolutionem sonat et consummationem, non solam effectionem; de qua multa Budæus in Comment.
anchorLine: τὰ ἐκείνης ἐσθίειν ἀνέχεται· οὔτε νεοτελὴς νοῦς (e)
en: 'Newly perfected mind.' As one recently initiated to perfection and having newly obtained it, though not yet sufficiently proved in it. Suidas: 'neoteles: newly completed'; which the Thesaurus ascribes to Hesychius, although it is only Suidas's, and renders it 'recently finished/absolved.' Portus's 'recently completed (confectus)' is not quite right. For that word, by which Suidas alone explained the other, signifies a kind of absolution and consummation, not merely making; on which Budaeus has much in his Commentary.

text: Ὁ Ἀμορῥαῖος. Sic nimirum Deut. i, 44, cum xiv, 45, non Amorrhæus, sed Amalec et Chananæus dicantur, sic de monte exsilientes, in quo erant in insidiis (ἐγκαθήμενοι) eos conscidisse ac persecutos esse, qui vim fecerant ut transirent: quod scilicet Deo irato rem aggrediebantur, Moyse etiam dissuadente. Ὁ οἰκῶν, quod scribit, qui habitabat, cum Hebr. ac reliquis convenit; potuitque sic haberi in Græcis, quorum illi copia fuit, sive erant τῶν LXX, sive ἡ κοινή. Quod est cap. 175, οὐχὶ πλῆθος τῶν κακῶν, nullus decoquere possim, ut ita scripsisse putem Maximum, aut forte habuisse cod. Vatic., nisi forte κακῶν, ἀντὶ τοῦ, πόνων positum sit. Sed præstaret καλῶν· honesti quippe nomine virtutis labores potius veniant, quam mali; iique uni quasi exercitus intelligantur, qui terrendo dæmones sint, nec vero terreant, nisi adsit, quam Maximus exigit virium animi una conspiratio et consensus.
anchorLine: ροδʹ. Πάλαι μὲν ὁ Ἀμοῤῥαῖος (e′) ἐν τῷ ὄρει οἰ-
en: 'The Amorite.' Thus, indeed, in Deut. i, 44, compared with Num. xiv, 45, it is not the Amorite but Amalek and the Canaanite who are said to have rushed down from the mountain, so that those lying in ambush on it (enkathemenoi) cut them down and pursued them, who had made an attempt to cross over, namely because they were undertaking the matter with God angry and Moses even dissuading them. The 'ho oikon' (the one dwelling), which he writes as 'who dwelt,' agrees with the Hebrew and the rest; and it could so have been read in the Greek copies, of which he had a supply, whether they were those of the Seventy or the common text. As in chapter 175, 'not a multitude of evils', which I cannot digest, so that I suppose Maximus wrote it so, or perhaps the Vatican codex had it, unless perhaps 'kakon' (of evils) is set for 'of toils (ponon)'. But 'kalon' (of good things) would be better: for the name of virtue would rather have toils be honorable than evil; and these alone are to be understood as an army, which would be terrifying the demons, and yet not terrify, unless there were present what Maximus requires: the single conspiracy and consensus of the soul's powers.

text: Ὑπὸ θηρὸς ὡς ὁ δηχθείς. Quin scriptum sit Maximo, ὑπὸ θηρὸς ὄφεως, nullus dubito. Sic enim θῆρες et θηρία (bestiæ scilicet) dicuntur Scripturæ phrasi, quæcunque animalia noxia, etiam ea, quæ vulgo insecta vocamus, cujusmodi sunt serpentes: uti etiam notavit Orig. in excerptis quæ exstant in Genesim, suntque a me collecta. Sic Act. xxviii, 4, de vipera Pauli manui adhærente, Ὡς δὲ εἶδον οἱ βάρβαροι κρεμάμενον τὸ θηρίον ἐκ τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ, Ut viderunt pendentem bestiam de manu ejus.
anchorLine: πηγάς, ὑπὸ [ὄφεως] θηρὸς ὡς ὁ δηχθείς (f)· ψυχὴ
en: 'By a beast, like one bitten.' I have no doubt that Maximus wrote 'by a beast of a serpent.' For in the phrase of Scripture, thēres and thēria (that is, beasts) are said of any noxious animals, even those we commonly call insects, such as serpents; as Origen too noted in the excerpts on Genesis which survive and were collected by me. So Acts xxviii, 4, of the viper clinging to Paul's hand: 'And when the barbarians saw the beast hanging from his hand.'

text: Ποῦ κοιτάζεις ἐν μεσημβρίᾳ τοὺς ἄρνας σου. Expressum ex Heb. [Hebrew word, not transcribed], quod est hiphil, ac proinde activam habet significationem, seu transitivam: quam potuit non mutare Syxt. interp. ea ipse religione, qua servaverant oἱ LXX. Idem peccat Gent. Hervetus in Greg. Nyssen. ad eum versum, ubi perinde reddit, ubi cubes; cum auctore Gregorio Sponsa sibi locum ostendi petat, in quo ipse Pastor bonus oves pascat, et accubare faciat. Eusebius quoque: Ἐὰν ἐν ταύτῃ με ποιμαίνῃς, κοιτάσῃς με πάντως ἐν μεσημβρίᾳ· Si me in salutari hac pascua paveris, prorsus in meridie collocabis: ἀντὶ τοῦ, Ἀναπαύσῃς ἐν τῷ ἀσκίῳ φωτὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως. Pro eo ac dicet Reficies, facies quiescere in loco resurrectionis, ubi nulla umbra est. Denique extra exemplum est, τὸ κοιτάζειν, ipsum esse τὸ, κοιτάζεσθαι, vel vocem cubare, aliam quam neutram ac intransitivam significationem habere. Hesych. κοιτάσαι, κατακοιμῆσαι· quod ipsum est, cubare facio, in lecto colloco; uti exponit Budæus: et ut alii metaphorice, sopio: suntque qui velint τὸ, κοιμῆσαι, pro κοιμίσαι scribi Æolice mutato ι in η. Est vero κομίσει eidem Hesych. κατακλίνει· quæ forma expressius activa est; etsi sunt alterius innumera exempla, ipsa pervia; haud forte satis illis animadversa, qui sic eam vocem quasi neutrali sensu, illique compositam τὸ, κοιτάσαι, acceperunt. Quæ sequitur vox in Maximo πεπλανημένη, errabunda, vagans, quomodo etiam habent Vulg. et versio Æthiopica, ipsa ex Græcis τῶν LXX expressa, in quibus interpres cum Maximo et ipse πεπλανημένη legerit; ni magis ut in Psello, illa vox expositio est ejus, quam ille habet, Maximus retinuit: Μήποτε γένωμαι ὡς παραβαλλομένη, πλανωμένη ἐπ᾽ ἀγέλης ἑτέρων σου· Ne fiam quasi decepta, vagabunda, errans, per occasionem gregis aliorum. Voxque Hebraica [Hebrew word, not transcribed] sic etiam exponitur; et non solum operuit, induit; quæ significatio haud satis huic loco congruit. Bene autem quam ex Psello, aliisque dixi. De Sponsa sermo est, sic sollicita inveniendi gregis Sponsi, et timentis in eo, per aliorum similitudinem, decipi, παραβαλεῖ· Hesych. ἀπατήσεις· decipies; hancque ejus vocis primam significationem ponit, ut notissimam et tritam. Suid. quoque, παραβλήδην, ἀπατητικῶς, παραλογιστικῶς. Nihilque ejus in eo occurrit ex Theucyd. quod Thesauri auctor studet elevare.
anchorLine: σημβρίᾳ τοὺς ἄρνας σου (f)· ἵνα τούτοις ἀκολου-
en: 'Where do you make your flock lie down at noon.' It is expressed from the Hebrew [Hebrew word], which is a hiphil and therefore has an active, that is transitive, signification; the Sixtine translator could have not changed it, with the same scruple with which the Seventy kept it. Gentian Hervet errs likewise in Gregory of Nyssa at that verse, where he renders it equally 'where you lie' (ubi cubes); whereas, on Gregory's authority, the Bride asks to be shown a place where the Good Shepherd himself pastures his sheep and makes them lie down. Eusebius also: 'If you shepherd me in this pasture, you will surely make me lie down at noon: that is, you will give me rest in the shadowless light of the resurrection'; in place of which he will say 'You will refresh, you will make rest in the place of the resurrection, where there is no shade.' Finally, it is unparalleled that koitazein should be the same as koitazesthai, or that the word 'to lie' should have a meaning other than neuter and intransitive. Hesychius: 'koitasai, katakoimesai,' which is, 'I make lie down, I put in a bed,' as Budaeus explains, and, as others, metaphorically, 'I put to sleep'; and there are those who would have koimesai written for koimisai with Aeolic change of iota to eta. And to the same Hesychius 'komisei' is 'kataklinei' (he lays down), a form more expressly active; though there are of the other usage innumerable examples, themselves open, not perhaps sufficiently noticed by those who took this word as if in neuter sense and compounded with it koitasai. The word that follows in Maximus, pepelanemene, 'wandering, straying', as the Vulgate and the Ethiopic version, itself drawn from the Seventy, have it, in which the translator along with Maximus himself read pepelanemene; unless rather, as in Psellus, that word is the explanation of the Hebrew which he has and Maximus retained: 'Lest I become as one thrown aside, wandering after the flock of your companions (Ne fiam quasi decepta, vagabunda, errans, by occasion of the flock of others).' And the Hebrew word is also thus explained; and not only 'covered, clothed,' a signification not well suited to this place. I have spoken well enough of this from Psellus and others. The subject is the Bride, so anxious to find her Bridegroom's flock and afraid of being deceived in it by likeness to others: 'parabalei' (Hesychius: 'apatēseis, you will deceive'); and he gives this as the first and well-known, common signification of the word. Suidas also: 'parablēdēn: deceitfully, fallaciously.' And nothing of it occurs in it from Thucydides, which the author of the Thesaurus tries to downplay.

text: Βόλοι δρόσου. Sic etiam vetera Lexica ex Greg. citant, habentque Græca Biblia, stillæ roris; ipsaque adeo Hebr. [Hebrew word, not transcribed] in qua voce Aben. Esra vult א esse formativum, quasi a [Hebrew word, not transcribed] ex eo quod stillæ ejusmodi rotundæ sint ac quasi convolutæ. Sic et βόλοι δρόσου, quod quasi globuli jaciantur, voce satis ingeniose excogitata τοῖς LXX. At quod Xyst. habent βῶλοι, glebæ roris, nullaque varia lectione interpr. affert, nullus probo; nec video quænam apta metaphora, ut roris stillæ, quod optime reddidit Vulg., dicantur glebæ. Quod etiam massa redditur ea vox, βῶλος σιδήρου Eccli. xxii, et βῶλος χρυσέα, pro sole, Apoll. Rhodii schol. ex Euripide, nihil congruit, quod massa, magni aliquid ponderis sit, non exile quid, uti stillæ roris: quarum stillare, spargi est et jaci, τὸ βάλλεσθαι.
anchorLine: σιʹ. Βόλοι μὲν δρόσου (g), γῆς μεθύσκουσιν αὔλα-
en: 'Drops (bolo) of dew.' So the old lexica cite it from Gregory too, and the Greek Bibles have 'drops of dew'; and so even the Hebrew [Hebrew word], in which word Aben Ezra would have the aleph be formative, as though from [Hebrew word], because such drops are round and as it were rolled together. So also 'bolo of dew,' as if little globes were thrown, a word quite ingeniously devised by the Seventy. But as for the Sixtine translators' having 'bolo,' clods of dew, and offering no variant reading, I do not approve; nor do I see what apt metaphor there is by which drops of dew would be called clods. That this word is also rendered 'mass' (bolos of iron in Ecclesiasticus xxii, and bolos of gold for the sun in the scholiast on Apollonius of Rhodes, from Euripides) is no support, since a mass is something of great weight, not something slight, like drops of dew, of which to drip, to be scattered, is to be cast, the verb ballesthai.

text: Καὶ τῆς γείτονος μονάδος. Videtur voce μονάδος significare, qua Deus unus ipse et singularis cognoscitur, nulla personarum distinctione; quam excedere necesse est, altiori cognitione, ut Deitatem in Trinitate intelligamus; et non solum δυάδα, binarium, qua voce Greg. Orat. in diem Natal. exque illo Maximus, creaturam intelligunt; quæ præsertim constant ex materia et forma. Vicinam dicit hanc μονάδα, quod proclive sit et innatum, ut sic Deum intelligamus. Est enim hæc inter ea quæ Paulus vocat nota Dei.
anchorLine: καὶ τῆς γείτονος μονάδος (h) ἄνωθεν μὴ ὀφθεὶς·
en: 'And of the neighboring monad.' He seems to mean by the word 'monad' that by which God is known as one and singular, without any distinction of persons; which must be transcended by a higher knowledge, so that we understand the Godhead in the Trinity; and not only the 'dyad', the 'binary', by which word Gregory in the Oration on the Nativity, and Maximus after him, understand the creature, which consists especially of matter and form. He calls this monad 'neighboring' because it is ready to hand and innate, that we may thus understand God. For it is among the things that Paul calls 'the known of God.'

text: Εἴσω τῶν ὁρωμένων. Id ita dictum Maximo videatur, quod mens ipsas eorum rationes in eis contempletur; et in illis τὰ ἀσώματα (res scilicet spiritales ac intelligibilia) cognoscat: ex quibus assurgit ad ipsum ὑπερούσιον Λόγον (Deum nimirum) quantum ex rebus a nobis cognosci potest. Sic cap. 589 et 590, ubi etiam necessario exigit, τὸ ἔξω γενέσθαι τῆς προσπαθείας τῶν αἰσθητῶν· ab omni terrenorum affectu excedere ac libidine, quo mentis illa puritas, de qua hic sermo est præstatur. Verum expeditius sit, scripsisse Maximum ἔξω τῶν ὁρωμένων· qua enim mente sic visibilibus excedimus, contemplando divina, terrena omnia, ac quidquid in illis dignum æmulatione videtur περιμάχητον, omnino contemnimus.
anchorLine: ὁρωμένων (i) παραπέμποντες, τοσούτου πίμπλανται
en: 'Within the things seen.' Maximus seems to have said this because the mind contemplates the very reasons of the things in them and knows in them the incorporeal things (that is, spiritual and intelligible realities), from which it rises to the supersubstantial Word himself (God, that is), as far as he can be known by us from things. So in chapters 589 and 590, where he likewise requires of necessity 'to be outside the sympathy of sensible things': to depart from all affection for earthly things and from lust, by which that purity of mind of which he speaks is secured. But it would be easier to say that Maximus wrote 'outside the things seen' (exo ton horomenon): for by that mind with which we thus pass beyond visible things in contemplating divine things, we altogether despise all earthly things and whatever in them seems worth contending for (perimachēton).

text: Ὁ φιλοκάλῳ πάθει. Quod φιλοκάλῳ τὸ φιλότιμον jungit Maximus, argumento est, sic in partem vitii illud usurpare, ut superfluum duntaxat cultum elegantiamque significet, cujus amor etiam iis qui ad pietatem exercent, obstaculo esse solet sublimioris volatus in oratione; quomodo ab Hesychio τὸ, φιλόκαλος, φιλόκοσμος exponitur: cum alioqui ea vox communius sonet in bonum, ac pro honesti studioso accipiatur: quandoque etiam dicatur de amore corporum. Sic φιλοκαλία Socrati objecta, ac si dictum fuisset παιδεραστία. Greg. de pavone perinde ambo hæc conjunxit φιλόκαλον καὶ φιλότιμον· ad notandum animal pulchritudinis amans, eaque sibi placens ac ambitiosum; ex quo Maximus transferre potuit in mores hominum.
anchorLine: ολάλῳ πάθει (j) καὶ φιλοτίμῳ κρατούμενος.
en: 'By a love-of-beauty passion.' That Maximus joins 'ambition' (philotimon) to 'love of the beautiful' (philokalo) is evidence that he takes the term in the sense of a vice, so that it denotes only superfluous adornment and elegance, the love of which is wont to be an obstacle even to those who practise piety, to a more sublime flight in prayer; as Hesychius explains 'philokalos' by 'philokosmos' (world-loving): though otherwise the word more commonly sounds in a good sense and is taken for one devoted to what is honorable; at times it is even said of the love of bodies. So 'philokalia' was charged against Socrates, as if it were said 'pederasty.' Gregory, concerning the peacock, likewise joined both: 'philokalon and philotimon', to mark an animal fond of beauty, pleased with itself and ambitious; from which Maximus could transfer it to the characters of men.

text: Διὰ τοῦ ἀποστερήματος. Sensus videtur, sic colendam pacem cum proximo, ut ejus causa omnem in eum patientiam exhibeamus, cujus ipsi nobis in Christo rei sumus; summam scilicet, ut quasi fraudatio Christianæ in nobis patientiæ sit, seu ex illa subtractio, quod sic in illum patientes simus. Sicut et fraudatio victus viduæ fuit, quod duo minuta ad necessarium usum reposita, sic in gazophylacium miserit; non superflua mittens, uti divites, sed ἐκ τοῦ ὑστερήματος αὐτῆς πάντα, quidquid in summa illa egestate illi suppetebat.
anchorLine: ἱς εἰρήνης, διὰ τοῦ ἀποστερήματος (k) τῆς ἐν Κυ-
en: 'Through the deprivation.' The sense seems to be that peace with one's neighbor is to be cultivated so that for his sake we show him all patience, of which we are ourselves guilty in Christ; the sum of it being that there should be, as it were, a defrauding of Christian patience in us, or a subtraction from it, in that we are thus patient toward him. As also the defrauding of the widow's livelihood was that she cast into the treasury two mites laid aside for necessary use; not sending in what was superfluous, like the rich, but 'out of her want' everything, whatever in that utmost poverty she had to support her.

text: Φαντασίαις οὐ σαλεύονται. Negatio omnino incommoda ac expungenda. Est enim caput istud, superioris quasi scholium; qua sæpius methodo Maximus utitur. Ei igitur qui prope ad ἀπάθειαν accedit, sed eam necdum perfecte adeptus est, id tribuit quod in vitiis minimum est; nudam scilicet cogitationem seu rei informationem; sicque deinceps reliqua reliquis; ad usque tactum, qui in sensibus crassior est, ac proinde summam denotat in rerum abusu exercitam libidinem; exstincta quasi arguente conscientia luceque rationis absorpta pro libidinis abundantia ac victoria: quod est sic ἀλύπως, nullo doloris sensu, in eo versari. Sic cap. 70, ἐμπάθειαν σώματος esse ait, et de illa tactum prædicari, ἁφήν· qui sensus maxime corporeus: ἡδυπάθεια vero, animæ; de qua prædicentur αἱ λοιπαὶ αἰσθήσεις, sensus reliqui; paulo scilicet spiritaliores; quorum minor vis quam ut omnino subjiciant animum, aut ejus omnem dolorem ex contrarii pugna auferant. Hos ait animo voluptarios σχέσεσι, affectibus commoveri; cap. vero 72, pati quidem illos interius ait, seu affici, sic tamen ut peccati vim (ἐνέργειαν) imbecilliorem ratione habeant. Sint fere ἡδυπαθεῖς, in quorum persona Paulus tanta de se loquitur Rom. vii, in quibus pugna illa legis mentis, ejusque, quæ in membris exsistit, id est concupiscentiæ: quam plerique non sentiunt, non quod ἀπαθεῖς, plene jam affectuum victores in tranquillitatis arce sint constituti; sed quod potius stupore ἐμπαθεῖς, sic illis mancipati, ut nec quod mancipati sunt, vero ullo animi sensu intelligant.
anchorLine: [οὐ] σαλεύονται (l)· ἐπιθυμίαις δὲ, οἱ μετριοπα-
en: 'They are not shaken by phantasies.' The negation is wholly awkward and ought to be deleted. For this chapter is, as it were, a scholion on the preceding one, by a method Maximus often uses. So to him who comes close to apatheia but has not yet perfectly attained it, he attributes what is least in vices: bare thought, or the forming of the thing in the mind; and so on in turn with the rest, up to touch, which is the coarser of the senses and therefore marks the highest degree of libido exercised in the abuse of things; it is quenched, as though conscience accused and the light of reason were swallowed up, by the abundance and victory of libido: that is, to be in it 'painlessly,' with no sense of pain. So in chapter 70 he says that the passion of the body is empathia, and that touch is predicated of it (haphe), the most corporeal sense; but hedypatheia (soft indulgence) belongs to the soul, of which the remaining senses are predicated, somewhat more spiritual, whose force is too small to subject the mind entirely or take away all its pain from the contrary struggle. These he says are moved in mind as voluptuaries by 'attachments' (schesesi), by affections; but in chapter 72 he says they suffer inwardly, that is are affected, yet so that they have the force (energeia) of sin weaker than reason. These would be roughly the hedypatheis, in whose person Paul says so much of himself in Rom. vii, in whom there is that struggle of the law of the mind and of that which exists in the members, that is, of concupiscence: which most do not feel, not because they are apathetic, already full victors set in the citadel of tranquillity, but rather because by stupor they are empatheis, so enslaved to them that they do not understand with any true sense of the mind that they are enslaved.

text: Εἰς τὸν τῆς μετριοπαθείας λιμένα. Non satis cohærere videtur, quod hic μετριοπάθειαν portum dicit, cum superius, c. 228, medios posuerit quos μετριοπαθεῖς vocat, eorum quos accedere ait ad
anchorLine: δύναται λιμένα (m) εἰσέρχεσθαι, ὁ βίᾳ τὰς
en: 'Into the harbor of moderation of passion.' It seems not quite consistent that he here calls metriopatheia a harbor, when above, chapter 228, he placed in the middle those whom he calls metriopatheis, of those whom he says approach to [continues on the next page].

text: ἀπάθειαν, et quos vocat ἡδυπαθεῖς· qui et jactentur ἐπιθυμίαις, cupiditatibus, desideriis. Portus enim, in quo tuta sit ac tranquilla statio, ἀπαθείας magis videatur, in qua non sit ullis jactari fluctibus, σαλεύεσθαι, sed pace frui ac quiescere. Nisi forte hoc vult Maximus, omnem nostram hic ἀπάθειαν, temperationem quamdam esse affectuum et μετριοπάθειαν· quorum motus nec perfectis desint, illisque jactari, cum tamen se illis abduci minime sinant, sintque velut navis ipsa in anchora σαλευομένη, tum etiam cum portum videtur tenere: ut nec tunc omne absit periculum, sed semper vigilare necesse sit, esseque cura sollicitum.
anchorLine: δύναται λιμένα (m) εἰσέρχεσθαι, ὁ βίᾳ τὰς
en: [the note begun on the preceding page continues:] apatheia, and whom he calls hedypatheis, who are also tossed by desires (epithymiai), cupidities. For a harbor, in which the station is safe and tranquil, would seem rather to belong to apatheia, in which one is not tossed (saleuesthai) by any waves but enjoys peace and rest. Unless perhaps Maximus means this: that our whole apatheia here is a certain tempering of the affections, and moderation of passion (metriopatheia); whose motions are not wanting even in the perfect, and they are tossed by them, though they by no means allow themselves to be carried away by them, and are like a ship itself riding at anchor (saleuomene), even when it seems to hold the harbor: so that not even then is all danger absent, but it is always necessary to be watchful, and to be anxious in care.

text: Οἱ δὲ συνδυάζονται. Addidi particulam δὲ, et sequentibus mutavi in καὶ· οἱ δὲ ἡδέως· οἱ καὶ ἡδέως· quod aperte tota loci structura ita exigat, sicque omnia plana sunt et expedita: sunt enim hæc duo membra per majorem explicationem sequentia. Porro saluberrima doctrina hæc, serio cavenda initia; paulatim malum augescere, ac tandem fieri insuperabile; scitumque exemplum est. τοῦ μονιοῦ ἀγρίου, singularis feri, id est, apri; qui et nobis inde sanglier dicitur: porcus scilicet silvester et solitarius; quem tenera ætate tantisper cohibeas; adultum vero, quin vineam demoliatur, intra quem admiseris, nulla industria compescere valeas. Sic autem psal. LXXIX, 14, idem animal significari utraque versiculi parte, esseque μονιὸν ἄγριον qui σῦς ἐκ δρυμοῦ multis ostendere conatur Bochart. lib. III, cap. 29, t. I Histor. animalium sacræ Scripturæ. Sic certe οἱ LXX accepere, ita reddendo, etsi Cyrillus ὄνον ἄγριον habet, uti etiam monuit Hesychi., quo etiam modo reddidit Arabicus, habentque Polyglot. Alii communius, bestiæ deserti, uti etiam Sym. ut sit potius genericum nomen τὸ, זיז significans bestiam, quam certæ alicujus speciei. Chald. Gallus silvester. R. David, fera, R. Salom. reptile. Aben. Esra, aves, volatilia. Longe aliter οἱ LXX, psal. XLIX, 11, ὡραιότης ἀγροῦ, species agri; cum sint eædem voces Hebraicæ, et series omnis de bestiis in genere seu animalibus silvestribus, poscat exponi. Hæc vero dicere speciem seu ornatum agri, seu deserti, id valde remotum, ac plane ænigmatice dictum videri possit. Schol. ex Sym. psal. illo LXXIX, ζῶα ἐρημίας, non bene refertur in Syxt. ad vocem σῦς ἐκ δρυμοῦ, qua certa species animalis in Græco pariter ac Hebr. denotatur, ipsa notissima; sed ad sequent. μονιὸς ἄγριος, cui respondet in Hebr. vox illa sic latæ significationis, et quæ omne animal significet; idemque sit ac Græcis κνώδαλον.
anchorLine: μη καθίστασθαι· οἱ δὲ συνδυάζονται (n) μὲν, ἁπλῶς
en: 'But they pair off.' I have added the particle 'de' and in what follows changed to 'kai': 'hoi de hedeos; hoi kai hedeos', because the whole structure of the passage plainly requires it, and so everything is smooth and clear: for these are two clauses following by a fuller explanation. Furthermore this is most salutary teaching: beginnings are to be earnestly guarded against; evil grows little by little and at last becomes insuperable; and the example is well known: 'the solitary wild beast' (monios agrios), 'a singular wild one,' that is, a boar, which is also called by us 'sanglier': a wild and solitary pig; which you may restrain for a time in its tender age; but once grown, you cannot, by any industry, restrain it from tearing down the vineyard into which you have admitted it. That in Psalm lxxix, 14, the same animal is signified in both halves of the verse, and that the 'monion agrion' is the 'sus ek drymou' (boar out of the wood), Bochart tries to show at length in book iii, chapter 29, vol. i of his History of the Animals of Sacred Scripture. So the Seventy certainly understood it in rendering it thus, although Cyril has 'wild ass' (onon agrion), as Hesychius too advised, and the Arabic rendered it in the same manner, and the Polyglot has it. Others more commonly render 'beast of the desert,' as Symmachus also, so that it is rather a generic noun, the Hebrew [ziz], signifying 'beast' rather than a certain species. The Chaldee: 'wild cock.' R. David: 'wild beast'; R. Solomon: 'reptile'; Aben Ezra: 'birds, fowl.' Quite differently the Seventy in Psalm xlix, 11, 'beauty of the field' (horaiotes agrou), 'species agri', although the Hebrew words are the same, and the whole sequence demands to be explained of beasts in general or of wild animals. To say 'form or ornament of the field, or of the desert' would seem very remote and plainly enigmatic. The scholion from Symmachus at that Psalm lxxix, 'creatures of the wilderness,' is not well referred in the Sixtine edition to the words 'sus ek drymou,' by which a definite species of animal is denoted, in Greek as in Hebrew, one very well known; but to the following 'monios agrios,' to which corresponds in the Hebrew that word of such wide signification, which could signify any animal; and which is the same as the Greek 'knodalon' (beast).

text: Τὸν τῆς κακοπαθείας σταυρόν. Vox passim Theologis recepta pro labore sponte assumpto et carnis afflictatione; in quo multi pene avidi, cum in immissis a Deo malis, ægre patientiam teneant; idque Maximus argute vocat κακοπαθείας clavos; qui scilicet, velimus nolimus, ac exteriore agente, cruci affigunt. Horum tolerantia probatur virtus; frustraque ejus nomine quis gloriatur ἐκτὸς θλίψεως, nisi ærumnam malaque passus; uti auctor est Marcus eremita De lege spirit. c. 66, ubi jam dixerat, c. 56, σύμβασιν ὀδυνηράν, casum molestum, Dei memoriam præbere; et 57, omnem ἀκούσιον πόνον. Ubi abstergendæ Obsop. sordes, si cha[...]a ferret, et locus.
anchorLine: ρὸν (ο) ἀνέρχονται· ὀλίγοι δὲ τοὺς ἥλους αὐτοῦ κατα-
en: 'The cross of suffering (kakopatheia).' A phrase commonly received among theologians for labor voluntarily undertaken and the affliction of the flesh; in which many are almost eager, although they hold patience hardly in the evils sent by God; and Maximus wittily calls these the nails of kakopatheia, which, whether we will or no, and with an outside agent, fasten us to the cross. The endurance of these proves virtue; and in vain does anyone glory in it who is outside of affliction, unless he has suffered hardship and ills; as Mark the hermit is authority in On the Spiritual Law, ch. 66, where he had already said, ch. 56, that a 'painful event' (symbasin odynēran), a troublesome occurrence, brings the memory of God; and in 57, every involuntary labor. Where, if the paper (?) would bear it, there would also be room for Obsopoeus's wiping away of stains. [The last sentence reads: 'Ubi abstergendæ Obsop. sordes, si cha[...]a ferret, et locus'; one word is not clear in the print.]

text: Ἐντελεῖς ὄντας. Erat fœdo errore in ἀπογράφῳ, ἀτελεῖς, nescio an in αὐτογράφῳ. Liquet certe nihil aptum, nec temere mihi indulsisse ut mutarem, atque mutando, Maximum Maximo redderem. De illis plane sermo est, qui cum sibi videantur jam virtutis arcem arripuisse, ac perfecti esse, genio sibi indulgendum putant, quasi superiori disciplina ultra non indigeant: quod nedum incauti spirituales ad corporis remissionem trahunt, in iis, quæ media esse possunt, verum etiam profani hæretici ad turpia, nefandasque libidines; quibus egregie cavet Maximus, tam sancto colophone finiens aurea sua, vereque ascetica, et ex Christi norma ad omnem virtutem firmantia, capita.
anchorLine: τοῦ φάρυγγος ἐντελεῖς ὄντας (p), ὅμοιόν τι ποιοῦσι
en: 'Being perfect.' There was a foul error in the copy: 'ateleis' (imperfect) — I do not know whether also in the autograph. It is clear at any rate that this was unfitting, and that I did not rashly indulge myself in changing it, and by the change restoring Maximus to Maximus. The talk is plainly of those who, since they seem to themselves to have already seized the citadel of virtue and to be perfect, think they must indulge their genius, as though they no longer needed stricter discipline: which not only the unwary spiritual draw to the relaxation of the body, in matters that can be indifferent, but even profane heretics to base and unspeakable lusts; against which Maximus guards superbly, ending his golden and truly ascetic chapters, which strengthen to all virtue from the rule of Christ, with so holy a colophon.

text: Dicti postea Bulgari, quorum hæc metropolis, ipsa Justiniana prima. Hujus operis altum aliis silentium, altissimo tamen Maximi ingenio compositum, vel hoc ipsum excerptum indicat, sic theologicum; ex Reg. cod. pridem exscriptum. Sed an jam tum βασιλεῖς Bulgariæ principes et reguli, quod eis tandem Græci concessere, dubium esse possit.
anchorLine: Ex opere LXIII Dubiorum, ad divinissimum Achridæ regem *.
en: [The Achrida mentioned] were afterwards called Bulgarians, whose metropolis this was, Justiniana Prima itself. Others are silent about this work, yet the excerpt itself indicates that it was composed by the very lofty genius of Maximus, theological as it is; it was transcribed some time ago from the Royal codex. But whether the princes and petty kings of Bulgaria were already then 'basileis' (kings), which the Greeks conceded to them only later, may be doubted.
